title: Six Alaskan ice-dammed lake gauge records (1948-2026) do not show one earlier-and-smaller outburst trend: Summit Lake did, Suicide Basin became later and larger
abstract: Veh et al. (2023) found that ice-dammed lake outbursts in north-western North America now occur earlier in the year and that the largest floods became smaller, from regional data to 2021. We tested this inside the records of single lakes and with new data for 2022-2026. We used public USGS daily discharge and peak-flow data for six Alaskan lakes: Summit Lake, Tulsequah Glacier lakes, Lake George, Hidden Creek Lake, Snow Lake and Suicide Basin. We extracted 113 outburst events that external references confirm (USGS code-9 peaks, a USGS 1987-2004 Taku table, an NWS 2025 Suicide Basin table). An unconstrained detector found the reference event in 88% of reference years. Outbursts became earlier at three lakes: Summit Lake (-1.50 d/yr, 95% interval -2.25 to -0.82), Tulsequah (-1.31 d/yr, a 33-day step near 2004) and Lake George before its outbursts stopped in 1966. Only Summit Lake outbursts became smaller (-0.0126 log10/yr; median excess 52,000 ft3/s in 1965-1972 and 12,600 ft3/s in 2010-2025). Hidden Creek Lake and Snow Lake had no clear timing change. Suicide Basin outbursts became later (+2.72 d/yr) and larger; in 2022-2026 they were about 1.8 times the size trend fitted to 2011-2021. NWS data show that the Suicide Basin release level fell 82 ft from 2016 to 2025 while the released volume more than doubled, so basin growth was larger than the effect of dam thinning. Trends fitted to data up to 2021 did not forecast 2022-2026 better than a recent mean, except Tulsequah timing. Limitations: six lakes, daily means, code-9 selection of annual peaks, a 1974-2008 data gap at Summit Lake, two source lakes at Taku, and provisional 2026 data. The package gives the USGS data snapshot with hashes, code, event tables, trend and test results, and three figures.

display.caption: Outburst day of year against year in six Alaskan ice-dammed lake records (USGS daily discharge, confirmed events). Black line: Theil-Sen trend of each lake. Orange dashed line: regional rate of Veh et al. (2023), about 49 days earlier in 121 years. Summit Lake and Tulsequah moved earlier; Suicide Basin moved later.

Log10 outburst excess (daily peak minus pre-event base flow) against year. Orange dashed line: one order of magnitude decrease in 121 years (Veh et al. regional extreme-flood rate). Only Summit Lake decreased; Suicide Basin and the Snow River gauge increased.

Left: Suicide Basin level at release start against released volume (NWS Juneau 2025 table); the release level fell while volume increased. Centre: Lake George outbursts came earlier from 1948 to 1966, then stopped. Right: Tulsequah outburst timing changed in a step near 2004.

citations.reason: Source of the regional earlier-and-smaller outburst trend that we test inside single-lake records and with 2022-2026 data. Our result supports earlier timing at some lakes but challenges a general size decrease within lakes.
Neal (2007), Table 1: Taku River outburst dates, source lakes, volumes and peaks for 1987-2004; transcribed as reference events.
USGS Snow River report: lower Snow Lake release levels, weak trend to higher peaks and no volume trend. Our gauge analysis agrees.
Kienholz et al. (2020): development of Suicide Basin and its outbursts since 2011.
NWS Juneau report, Table 1: Suicide Basin outburst dates, volumes and basin levels at release start for 2011-2025.
NWS Juneau Suicide Basin page, accessed 2026-11-12: August 2026 event and second release on 2026-10-02.
